questions.stem: In the food chain maize → grasshopper → toad → snake, the toad is a
questions.explanation: Maize is the producer and the grasshopper that eats it is the primary consumer. The toad eats the grasshopper, so it is a secondary consumer occupying the third trophic level. A decomposer would be a bacterium or fungus acting on dead remains, not a link in this chain.

distractorRationale.a: Only the maize photosynthesises, so only it is the producer
distractorRationale.b: The grasshopper, not the toad, is the herbivore and primary consumer
distractorRationale.d: The toad is a carnivore, not a decomposer

questions.stem: Approximately what percentage of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next?
questions.explanation: The ten-per-cent rule is the WAEC working figure: only about one tenth of the energy stored at a trophic level becomes biomass at the next. The other 90% is lost as heat from respiration, as uneaten material and as faeces, which is why food chains stay short.

distractorRationale.a: 1% is far too low for the standard transfer figure used in secondary biology
distractorRationale.c: Half the energy is not passed on; most is lost as heat
distractorRationale.d: 90% is the fraction lost, not the fraction transferred

sources.title: WAEC Biology Syllabus — Food Chains and Energy Flow

questions.stem: The arrows in a food chain represent the

options.text: order in which the organisms evolved
decrease in the number of organisms

questions.explanation: Each arrow points from the organism that is eaten towards the organism that eats it, which is the path energy takes. Writing the chain backwards, or thinking the arrow means 'is eaten by' in the opposite direction, is a standard exam error.

distractorRationale.a: Food chains are about feeding, not migration
distractorRationale.c: Evolution is not shown by food-chain arrows
distractorRationale.d: Numbers may fall along a chain, but that is not what the arrow itself stands for

sources.title: WAEC Biology Syllabus — Food Chains and Energy Flow

questions.stem: Which ecological pyramid is always upright?
questions.explanation: Energy is lost as heat at every transfer, so the energy content of each trophic level is always less than the one below it. Numbers and biomass can invert — one tree supporting many insects, or fast-growing phytoplankton supporting a larger mass of zooplankton — but energy cannot increase up the chain.

distractorRationale.a: A single tree with many herbivores inverts a pyramid of numbers
distractorRationale.b: Biomass pyramids can invert in aquatic systems with rapid phytoplankton turnover
distractorRationale.d: There is no standard pyramid of species in this topic

sources.title: WAEC Biology Syllabus — Food Chains and Energy Flow

questions.stem: Most of the energy taken in by a toad is not passed on to the snake that eats it because the energy is

options.text: used in respiration and lost as heat, or left in uneaten and egested material
converted into carbon dioxide that the snake cannot use
stored permanently in the toad's bones

questions.explanation: Energy is not destroyed, but it changes form. Respiration releases much of it as heat that leaves the food chain, and the snake never receives the energy in parts it does not eat or in faeces. That combined loss is why transfer is only about 10%.

distractorRationale.a: Energy cannot be destroyed; it is converted, mostly to heat
distractorRationale.c: Carbon dioxide is a respiratory product, not a store of the toad's food energy for the snake
distractorRationale.d: Bone is uneaten material, but energy is not locked there permanently as a special store

questions.stem: Bacteria and fungi that feed on dead leaves in a cocoa plantation are best described as
questions.explanation: Decomposers break down dead organic matter and release mineral nutrients that producers can reuse. They are not a single trophic level in the chain; they act on remains from every level. They do not photosynthesise, so they are not producers.

distractorRationale.a: Producers are green plants and algae that photosynthesise
distractorRationale.b: Primary consumers are herbivores that eat living plant material
distractorRationale.d: Tertiary consumers are carnivores near the top of a chain

questions.stem: A pyramid of numbers for a mango tree, the caterpillars feeding on it, and the birds feeding on the caterpillars is inverted at the base. This is because

options.text: energy increases from the tree to the caterpillars
one large producer supports many small primary consumers
birds are more numerous than caterpillars

questions.explanation: Numbers count individuals, not size. A single tree is one organism, so the producer bar is tiny, while thousands of caterpillars make a wide bar above it. Energy still decreases from tree to caterpillar to bird, so a pyramid of energy for the same system remains upright.

distractorRationale.a: Energy never increases up a food chain
distractorRationale.c: Birds are fewer than caterpillars; that is why the top of this numbers pyramid narrows again
distractorRationale.d: A mango tree is a photosynthetic producer

sources.title: WAEC Biology Syllabus — Food Chains and Energy Flow

questions.stem: If producers in a pond capture 10 000 kJ of energy, about how much energy would be available to a tertiary consumer, assuming 10% transfer at each step?
questions.explanation: Primary consumers receive about 10% of 10 000 kJ = 1 000 kJ. Secondary consumers receive 10% of that = 100 kJ. Tertiary consumers receive 10% of 100 kJ = 10 kJ. Three transfers separate the producer from the tertiary consumer, which is why top carnivores are rare.

distractorRationale.a: 1 000 kJ is the energy at the primary-consumer level, after only one transfer
distractorRationale.b: 100 kJ is the energy at the secondary-consumer level
distractorRationale.d: 1 kJ would require a fourth transfer, to a quaternary consumer

questions.stem: In a food web, which of the following organisms would be classified as a secondary consumer?
questions.explanation: A secondary consumer is an organism that eats primary consumers. In this case, the toad feeds on the grasshopper, making it a secondary consumer in the food web.

distractorRationale.a: Grass is a producer, not a consumer.
distractorRationale.b: Grasshopper is a primary consumer, feeding on plants.
distractorRationale.d: Snake is a tertiary consumer, as it feeds on the toad.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why energy decreases as it moves up trophic levels?

options.text: Energy is lost as heat during metabolic processes.

questions.explanation: As energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next, a significant portion is lost as heat due to metabolic processes, which explains the decrease in available energy at higher levels.

distractorRationale.b: While there are fewer organisms at higher levels, this does not directly explain energy loss.
distractorRationale.c: Higher trophic levels do not consume more energy; they receive less.
distractorRationale.d: Energy is not solely stored; it is also lost during energy transfer.
